questions.text:
Consider routing table of an organization's router shown below:
[latex] \begin{array}{|l|l|l|} Subnet Number & Subnet Mask & Next Hop \\ 12.20.164.0 & 255.255.252.0 & R1 \\ 12.20.170.0 & 255.255.254.0 & R2 \\ 12.20.168.0 & 255.255.254.0 & Interface 0 \\ 12.20.166.0 & 255.255.254.0 & Interface 1 \\ default & ~ & R3 \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]
Which of the following prefixes in CIDR notation can be collectively used to correctly aggregate all of the subnets in the routing table?
questions.solution:
Third-octet ranges of the subnets:
- 164.0/22 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 164-167
- 166.0/23 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 166-167 (inside the first)
- 168.0/23 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 168-169
- 170.0/23 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 170-171

Together they cover 164-171. 12.20.164.0/22 covers 164-167 and 12.20.168.0/22 covers 168-171, exactly the needed range.

164.0/21 is really 160-167 (not aligned) and /20 is 160-175, both covering addresses that are not in the table.

Answer: 12.20.164.0/22 and 12.20.168.0/22

questions.text: Consider the resolution of the domain name [latex]www.gate.org.in[/latex] by a DNS resolver. Assume that no resource records are cached anywhere across the DNS servers and that iterative query mechanism is used in the resolution. The number of DNS query-response pairs involved in completely resolving the domain name is .
questions.solution:
With iterative resolution and empty caches, the resolver asks each level in turn:
1. Root server [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] refers to the .in server
2. .in server [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] refers to org.in
3. org.in server [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] refers to gate.org.in
4. gate.org.in server [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] returns the IP of www.gate.org.in

Answer: 4

questions.text:
Consider an enterprise network with two Ethernet segments, a web server and a firewall, connected via three routers as shown below.

What is the number of subnets inside the enterprise network?
questions.solution:
Every link between router interfaces (and every LAN behind a router) is a separate subnet:
1. Firewall - left router
2. Firewall - top router
3. Top router - web server
4. Top router - right router
5. Left router - left Ethernet
6. Right router - right Ethernet

Answer: 6

questions.text: Consider a network using the pure ALOHA medium access control protocol, where each frame is of length 1,000 bits. The channel transmission rate is 1 Mbps (=[latex]10^6[/latex] bits per second). The aggregate number of transmissions across all the nodes (including new frame transmissions and retransmitted frames due to collisions) is modelled as a Poisson process with a rate of 1,000 frames per second. Throughput is defined as the average number of frames successfully transmitted per second. The throughput of the network (rounded to the nearest integer) is ______________
questions.solution:
Frame time T = 1000 / [latex]10^6[/latex] = 1 ms. Load G = 1000 frames/s [latex]\times[/latex] 1 ms = 1.

Pure ALOHA success probability = [latex]e^{-2G}=e^{-2}\approx0.135[/latex].
Throughput = 1000 [latex]\times[/latex] 0.135 [latex]\approx[/latex] 135 frames/s

Answer: 135

questions.text:
Consider a computer network using the distance vector routing algorithm in its network layer. The partial topology of the network is shown below.

The objective is to find the shortest-cost path from the router R to routers P and Q. Assume that R does not initially know the shortest routes to P and Q. Assume that R has three neighboring routers denoted as X, Y and Z. During one iteration, R measures its distance to its neighbors X, Y, and Z as 3, 2 and 5, respectively. Router R gets routing vectors from its neighbors that indicate that the distance to router P from routers X, Y and Z are 7, 6 and 5, respectively. The routing vector also indicates that the distance to router Q from routers X, Y and Z are 4, 6 and 8 respectively. Which of the following statement(s) is/are correct with respect to the new routing table o R, after updation during this iteration?
questions.solution:
Cost via each neighbour = (R to neighbour) + (neighbour's distance):
- To P: X 3 + 7 = 10, Y 2 + 6 = 8, Z 5 + 5 = 10 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 8 via Y
- To Q: X 3 + 4 = 7, Y 2 + 6 = 8, Z 5 + 8 = 13 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 7 via X

So R-P is 8 via Y (not 10), and R-Q is 7 via X (not via Z).

Answer: Distance to Q is 7; next hop to P is Y

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: The distance from R to P will be stored as 10
The distance from R to Q will be stored as 7
The next hop router for a packet from R to P is Y
The next hop router for a packet from R to Q is Z
